prompt_latex: \text{Prove that }T(x, y) = (2x - y, x + 3y)\text{ is a linear transformation.}
prompt_plain: Prove that T(x, y) = (2x − y, x + 3y) is a linear transformation.

prompt_parts.text: Prove that T(x, y) = (2x − y, x + 3y) is a linear transformation.

worked_solution: Let u = (x₁, y₁), v = (x₂, y₂) and k be a scalar
T(u + v) = (2(x₁ + x₂) − (y₁ + y₂), (x₁ + x₂) + 3(y₁ + y₂)) = (2x₁ − y₁, x₁ + 3y₁) + (2x₂ − y₂, x₂ + 3y₂) = T(u) + T(v)
T(ku) = (2kx₁ − ky₁, kx₁ + 3ky₁) = k(2x₁ − y₁, x₁ + 3y₁) = kT(u)
Both properties hold, so T is linear

prompt_parts.text: Is A = [2 1 0; 0 2 0; 0 0 3] diagonalisable?

worked_solution: A is triangular, so the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: λ = 2 (twice) and λ = 3
This has rank 2, so the eigenspace has dimension 3 − 2 = 1
λ = 2 has algebraic multiplicity 2 but only 1 independent eigenvector
That is 2 independent eigenvectors in total for a 3×3 matrix, so A is not diagonalisable
final_answer: Not diagonalisable (eigenvalue 2 has only a 1-dimensional eigenspace)

prompt_latex: \text{Find the eigenvalues of }A = \begin{bmatrix}4&0&1\\2&3&2\\1&0&4\end{bmatrix}\text{ and decide if A is diagonalisable.}

prompt_parts.text: Find the eigenvalues of A = [4 0 1; 2 3 2; 1 0 4] and decide if A is diagonalisable.

worked_solution: Expand det(A − λI) along column 2: (3 − λ) · det[4−λ 1; 1 4−λ]
λ = 3: A − 3I = [1 0 1; 2 0 2; 1 0 1] has rank 1, so the eigenspace has dimension 3 − 1 = 2, spanned by (0, 1, 0) and (−1, 0, 1)
Eigenspace dimensions 2 + 1 = 3, so there are 3 independent eigenvectors: A is diagonalisable
